text: Once Transform hands you a clean DataFrame, where does it actually go? This lesson covers the three real options for a Load target, and introduces the tool this chapter's pipeline will actually use for the rest of the chapter.

A file — CSV, JSON, Parquet — is simple and portable with no server required. A database, like a real AdventureWorks2012 instance, uses the same pyodbc and SQLAlchemy patterns from Chapter 5. And a warehouse is just a database built for analytics at scale, loaded the exact same way from Python's point of view.

Requiring every student to run a full SQL Server instance just to follow along isn't realistic, so this chapter uses SQLite as a lighter stand-in for that warehouse target. It's real, serverless, and file-based, built right into Python. load_to_warehouse connects to a local .db file and calls df.to_sql with if underscore exists equals replace — and that to_sql call works exactly the way it did against the real SQLAlchemy engine back in Lesson 30.

Loading isn't done the moment the write finishes — confirm it. count_rows runs a simple SELECT COUNT star against the target table. Checking that the row count matches what you expected to load is a cheap habit that catches a surprising number of real pipeline bugs.

Here's the part that matters most: if this pipeline were pointed at a real SQL Server warehouse instead of SQLite, the to_sql call barely changes. Swap in a SQLAlchemy engine pointed at AdventureWorks2012, keep the same DataFrame, same method call. The rest of the pipeline doesn't need to know or care which one it's writing to.
Right now, every run of this pipeline reloads the entire dataset from scratch. That's fine at twenty rows. Next lesson tackles why that stops being fine at scale, and introduces watermarks to fix it.
